title: The Early Date of the New Testament
short: the early dating of the New Testament

keyTerms.d: A document produced within the lifetime of eyewitnesses is too early to be a fully developed legend that could circulate unchallenged. The conclusion is modest: it tells us the material is early, not that it is accurate.

The Oxford Roman historian A. N. Sherwin-White, working from how legends actually behave in the ancient sources, argued that even two full generations was too short an interval for legend to wipe out a solid historical core. Critics such as Richard Carrier note, accurately, that this was an observation drawn from a particular body of Greek material, not a demonstrated law of folklore; the premise needs only the comparative point that more time and more distance make undetected legend easier.

In 1 Corinthians 15:3–7, writing in the mid-50s, Paul hands on what he himself had “received.” The technical language of “delivering” and “receiving” tradition, the non-Pauline vocabulary, the rhythmic structure, and the Aramaic name Cephas mark it out as a pre-formed oral creed that Paul is quoting, not composing.

Romans, the Corinthian correspondence, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon are dated by near-universal agreement to roughly AD 48–60. They already presuppose the central narrative of cross and resurrection — which establishes early attestation, how soon the claims are on record, not by itself that their content is true.

Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome and never reports the deaths of Paul, Peter or James the brother of Jesus, the Neronian persecution, or the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. On this reading Luke wrote Acts in the early 60s — but it is genuinely an argument from silence, only as strong as the certainty that the author would have mentioned the missing event.

A “prophecy after the fact.” The mainstream view reads Jesus’s prediction of Jerusalem’s destruction in Mark 13 as most simply explained by an Evangelist writing after AD 70 and shaping the prophecy in light of what had occurred. It is not special pleading as a method, but the inference is far less decisive than it sounds.

A document cannot be later than the first author who quotes it, and 1 Clement, Ignatius and Polycarp already treat New Testament writings as known and authoritative. What this shows is a ceiling, not a floor: it rules out composition centuries after Jesus, but it does not decide between the mainstream dates and the earlier ones.

The finding, from a scholar who set out to disprove it, that the Gospels were composed in the genre of ancient biography, a literary form whose purpose is to convey historical information about a real person. That is a claim about genre, not a guarantee of accuracy: ancient bioi still selected and shaped their material around a theme.

derive.q: Paul quotes a creed he “received,” and the tradition must predate his Jerusalem visit three years after his conversion — so its content dates…?
derive.ans: within a few years of the crucifixion
derive.why: Paul’s own conversion is usually placed within a few years of the crucifixion, and in Galatians 1:18–19 he meets Cephas and James — two of the named witnesses in the creed — three years later. The tradition he relays must predate that meeting. That is why the dating crosses ideological lines: even Gerd Lüdemann, who rejects a bodily resurrection, dates its elements to “the first two years after the crucifixion… not later than three years.”

derive.q: Acts never reports Paul’s death, James’s death (AD 62) or Jerusalem’s fall — so on this reading it was written…?
derive.ans: in the early 60s — on a contested argument from silence
derive.why: Luke narrates the martyrdom of Stephen at length, records that of James son of Zebedee, and returns again and again to the Temple, so he would have had every reason to mention these catastrophes had they already happened. A convergence of expected-yet-absent events is more telling than any single omission. But it is genuinely an argument from silence, and Luke may have ended Acts where his narrative purpose was complete.

derive.q: Mark 13 says nothing of the fire, the months-long siege or Titus’s legions — so the after-the-fact reading is…?
derive.ans: far less decisive than it sounds
derive.why: The prediction is conspicuously unspecific about the manner of Jerusalem’s fall, omitting the very details a writer narrating after the fact would find hard to omit, and its most vivid imagery is drawn from Scripture, not from the events of 70. This is why E. P. Sanders, for all his post-70 dating of the Gospels, judged Mark’s prediction of the Temple’s destruction “probably pre-70.”

derive.q: Grant the mainstream date of Mark, c. AD 70. Does the early date of the central proclamation fall with it…?
derive.ans: no — the creed and Paul’s letters are early regardless
derive.why: The early-dating case for the central claims does not stand or fall with Mark’s date at all. Even on Ehrman’s own chronology, the creed of 1 Corinthians 15 and Paul’s letters carry the death, burial, and resurrection proclamation back into the 30s and 50s. Whether Mark is 65 or 72 changes little here.

derive.q: 1 Clement, Ignatius and Polycarp already cite New Testament writings as authorities — so their testimony fixes…?
derive.why: A document cannot be later than the first author who quotes it. On the usual dates these writings were known within about eighty years of the crucifixion, and even the latest proposals push that only into the 130s and 140s. It does not decide between the mainstream dates and the earlier ones, since even the earliest proposed date for these writers is no earlier than about 70.

derive.q: Grant every early date. Does that show that what the documents say is true…?
derive.ans: no — early does not mean true
derive.why: An early date rules out one explanation — slow, undetected legendary development — but it does not rule out sincere error or deliberate fabrication; people can and do invent things quickly. The argument removes a whole class of objection and hands the central claims over to be assessed as first-generation testimony, where honesty, accuracy, and the resurrection itself are taken up on their own terms.

honestState.p1: On the dating of the four Gospels, the mainstream consensus — articulated by Bart Ehrman among many others: Mark c. 70, Matthew and Luke c. 80–85, John c. 90–95 — remains the majority view, and E. P. Sanders judged the Gospels probably composed between 70 and 90. The pre-70 dating championed by John A. T. Robinson and Colin Hemer, and restated more recently by Alexander Mittelstaedt, Karl Armstrong and David Seccombe, is a respected minority position, not the field’s settled judgment; a centrist commentator like Craig Keener, no partisan of the early date, still places Luke–Acts in the early 70s, with the 60s and 80s among the live possibilities. From the other side, a smaller group, the fullest statement is Richard Pervo’s, with Joseph Tyson supplying a setting, places Acts in the early second century. But on the dating of the earliest tradition — the 1 Corinthians 15 creed and the undisputed Pauline letters — there is broad agreement across the ideological spectrum, skeptics included, that the material is remarkably early.
honestState.fairness: Honest defenders must grant the observations: the vaticinium ex eventu reading is not special pleading as a method, and the correspondence between Jesus’s words and the events of 70 is real; the argument from silence in Acts is genuinely an argument from silence, and Luke may have ended Acts where his narrative purpose was complete; Sherwin-White’s “two-generation rule” is an observation, not a demonstrated law of folklore; Habermas’s survey is a count of published positions assembled by one researcher, not a randomized poll; and the creed does not date the Gospels. None of that carries the critic’s inference. Mark 13 is conspicuously unspecific about the manner of Jerusalem’s fall, a convergence of expected-yet-absent events is more telling than any single omission, and the early-dating case for the central claims does not stand or fall with Mark’s date at all.
honestState.verdict: The foundational Christian claims about Jesus’s death and resurrection appearances are not the residue of generations of mythmaking; they are demonstrably early, fixed in creedal form within a few years of the events, named to specific witnesses, and circulated while hostile parties in Jerusalem could have objected. Even on the mainstream (later) dating, the Gospels fall within living memory, and the “legend had time to grow” hypothesis, in its strong form, does not fit the evidence. The pre-70 dating of the narrative Gospels remains a serious, defensible, but genuinely contested position — not a settled result. And early does not mean true: the argument clears the ground and hands the central claims over to be assessed as first-generation testimony, where the resurrection itself is argued on its own evidence — and this Library defends the inference that Jesus rose bodily from the dead.

order: A document produced within the lifetime of eyewitnesses is too early to be a fully developed legend that could circulate unchallenged.
The core New Testament material falls inside that eyewitness window — and its earliest layers, Paul’s undisputed letters of the 50s and the 1 Corinthians 15 creed, fall startlingly early.
Therefore the New Testament must be assessed not as late mythology but as first-generation testimony — which tells us it is early, not that it is accurate.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and how modest its conclusion is.
cards.a: A document produced within the lifetime of eyewitnesses is too early to be a fully developed legend that could circulate unchallenged. The conclusion is modest: it tells us the material is early, not that it is accurate.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and what it does NOT require.
cards.a: The core New Testament material falls inside the eyewitness window, and its earliest layers — Paul’s undisputed letters of the 50s and the 1 Corinthians 15 creed — fall startlingly early. It does not require the most aggressive possible dating of the four Gospels; the strongest version rests on the layers the great majority of scholars, believer and skeptic alike, already grant to be early.

cards.q: What does an early date rule out — and what does it leave standing?
cards.a: It rules out one explanation: slow, undetected legendary development. It does not rule out sincere error or deliberate fabrication, because people can and do invent things quickly — those questions are taken up on their own terms.

cards.q: What marks 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 as a creed Paul is quoting rather than composing?
cards.a: The technical language of “delivering” and “receiving” tradition, the non-Pauline vocabulary, the rhythmic structure, and the Aramaic name Cephas. Together they mark a pre-formed oral formula already circulating before Paul wrote it down.

cards.q: Why does the creed’s early date cross ideological lines — and what caution goes with the survey figure?
cards.a: The tradition must predate Paul’s Jerusalem meeting with two of its named witnesses three years after his conversion, and even a scholar who rejects a bodily resurrection dates its elements to “the first two years after the crucifixion… not later than three years.” The survey of scholarly support is a count of published positions assembled by one researcher, not a randomized poll, and should be cited with care.

cards.q: What do Paul’s undisputed letters establish — and not establish?
cards.a: Dated by near-universal agreement to roughly AD 48–60, they are first-generation documents that already presuppose the central narrative of cross and resurrection, placing the load-bearing claims well inside living memory. That establishes early attestation — how soon the claims are on record — not, by itself, that their content is true.

cards.q: Why do the silences of Acts point to an early date — and what is the limit?
cards.a: Acts never reports Paul’s death, James’s death or Jerusalem’s fall, though Luke narrates other martyrdoms and returns again and again to the Temple; a convergence of expected-yet-absent events is more telling than any single omission. Limit: it is genuinely an argument from silence, and Luke may have ended Acts where his narrative purpose was complete.

cards.q: Which arguments for an early Acts do NOT turn on silence — and how strong are they?
cards.a: The political climate (Luke’s salvation cast in the terms of Israel’s national hope fits more naturally before the Jewish revolt) and the book’s purpose (its long case for receiving Gentiles presupposes a Jewish church in the position of strength). Both are contested, and are offered as further, cumulative reasons rather than a proof — but they point to positive features of the text rather than gaps in it.

cards.q: Why does the mainstream date Mark around AD 70 — and is that special pleading?
cards.a: Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source, so Mark circulated first, and Mark 13’s prediction of Jerusalem’s destruction is read as written after the event. It is not special pleading as a method — historians as a rule do not assume genuine foreknowledge when an ordinary explanation is available — but the inference is far less decisive than it sounds.

cards.q: Why is the after-the-fact reading of Mark 13 less decisive than it sounds?
cards.a: The prediction is conspicuously unspecific — nothing of the fire, the months-long siege or Titus’s legions — and its most vivid imagery is drawn from Scripture, not from the events of 70. Nor does predicting the Temple’s fall require foreknowledge to be early: Josephus reports another Jesus crying woe on the city and sanctuary from AD 62, years before the war.

cards.q: What does the “latest possible date” argument show — and not show?
cards.a: Early Christian writers already quote New Testament writings as authorities, which sets a ceiling, not a floor: it rules out composition centuries after Jesus but does not decide between the mainstream dates and the earlier ones. Like every argument here, it shows that the writings existed and were valued early, not that what they say is true.

cards.q: Is the case for a second-century Acts made?
cards.a: No. Its central link to Josephus is disputed at its strongest point, its argument from Paul’s letters is at least as well explained by an author who knew Paul, and its affinities fit at least as well with a book written earlier and used later. The live question is whether Acts was written in the early 60s or in the decades after 70.

obj.q: The standard consensus, articulated by Bart Ehrman among many others, puts Mark around AD 70 and Matthew and Luke in the 80s. Matthew and Luke used Mark, and Mark 13 (the Olivet Discourse) and its parallels have Jesus predicting the encirclement and destruction of Jerusalem — the simplest explanation is a prophecy after the fact, and Luke 21:20’s “surrounded by armies” reads as written with the siege in view. Your early dates multiply improbabilities to avoid the obvious.
obj.model: The method is fair — historians do not assume genuine foreknowledge when an ordinary explanation is available, and Mark as one of Luke’s sources is granted. But the inference is far less decisive than it sounds. Mark 13 is conspicuously unspecific about the manner of Jerusalem’s fall, saying nothing of the fire, the months-long siege or the legions of Titus; this is why E. P. Sanders, for all his post-70 dating of the Gospels, judged Mark’s prediction “probably pre-70.” Its most vivid imagery is drawn from Scripture, and Luke’s “surrounded by armies” is the stock language of any siege — C. H. Dodd argued Luke’s picture is drawn from the Old Testament accounts of Jerusalem’s fall in 587 BC. Nor does a prediction of the Temple’s fall require foreknowledge to be early: Josephus reports another Jesus, son of Ananias, crying woe on the city from AD 62. Most importantly, the early-dating case for the central claims does not stand or fall with Mark’s date: even on Ehrman’s own chronology, the creed of 1 Corinthians 15 and Paul’s letters carry the death, burial, and resurrection proclamation back into the 30s and 50s. So the post-70 inference does not settle the matter: the pre-70 dating of the Gospels remains a serious, defensible, but genuinely contested position, and the central claims are early either way.

obj.q: As Bart Ehrman would put it: you have rescued the early creed, granted, but you have not rescued the early Gospels. It is the Gospels that contain the miracles, the empty tomb, the detailed narratives — so the gap you most needed to close, you have left open.
obj.model: The first half is accurate: the creed does not date the Gospels. The second is not, because the argument never promised to close that gap. What the creed establishes is that the explanatory core — a crucified, buried, and risen Jesus, as the creed proclaims him, attested by named witnesses — is too early to be slow legend. The narrative details are a further question, addressed by other lines of evidence, including the case that the Gospels themselves rest on named eyewitness testimony, and the finding that they were composed in the genre of Graeco-Roman biography. That is a claim about genre, not a guarantee of accuracy: ancient bioi still selected and shaped their material around a theme. But it means the Gospels ask to be read as testimony about a real life, not as free-floating myth. So the objection does not hold against what the argument actually claims.

obj.q: Richard Pervo places Acts around AD 115: Luke used Josephus’s Antiquities (AD 93/94) and garbled it — Gamaliel’s Theudas and Judas (Acts 5:36–37) — knew a collection of Paul’s letters, and shares vocabulary with second-century writers. Joseph Tyson adds that Luke–Acts was finished around 120–125 as a response to Marcion.
obj.model: Its supports are weaker than they look. The Josephus case leans hardest on a passage where Acts and Josephus disagree: the real difficulty is that Gamaliel, speaking in the 30s, sets Theudas before Judas, whereas Josephus’s Theudas rose a decade or more later — a recognised historical problem, but however it is resolved, Josephus’s sequence does not explain it. As Jonathan Bernier has argued, using a place where Luke diverges from Josephus to prove that Luke used Josephus exposes how weak the hypothesis is. The question is not closed — Steve Mason thinks Luke probably did know Josephus — but even if he did, that would place Acts after the mid-90s, not establish a date around 115. Acts never says that Paul wrote letters and never quotes one, and a writer who had heard Paul preach, as the “we” passages present the narrator, would not need a letter collection. Shared vocabulary may mean that later writers drew on Acts, or simply that one church idiom ran across a few decades. And the themes Tyson reads as anti-Marcionite already have a first-century occasion in the disputes over Gentile inclusion; Tyson’s reconstruction also rests on a contested premise — that Marcion used an earlier form of Luke which our Gospel revised — whereas Irenaeus, writing around 180, reports that Marcion cut down the Gospel according to Luke. So the case for a second-century date is not made: the evidence leaves Acts where most scholars place it: in the first century.

obj.q: Your premise leans on Sherwin-White’s “two-generation rule,” but as Richard Carrier and others point out, that was an observation drawn from a particular body of Greek material, not a law of folklore. Legends can grow fast — so a short window proves nothing.
obj.model: That much is accurate: rapid legendary embellishment is not impossible, and the rate at which stories mutate varies enormously. But Premise One does not need an iron law. It needs only the comparative point that more time and more distance make undetected legend easier — and the New Testament window is unusually tight by the standards of ancient history, where our best surviving biographies of Alexander the Great, by Arrian and Plutarch, were written some four centuries after him and are still mined for a historical core. At the foundation the window is tighter still: the central claims were fixed in creedal form within a few years of the events, named to specific witnesses, and circulated while hostile parties in Jerusalem could have objected. What that rules out is slow, undetected legendary development — not sincere error or deliberate fabrication, which are weighed on their own terms. So the objection trims an overstated rule; it does not remove the premise.

unseen.q: You call Paul a checkable link back to the eyewitnesses. But Paul insists the gospel he preached was “not man’s gospel” and came “through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:11–12). By his own account Peter did not teach it to him — so the chain you are building through Jerusalem is not there.
unseen.model: Paul does say that, and we should not overstate what the Jerusalem contacts show: this is not a report of Paul being taught the tradition by Peter, nor of the eyewitnesses auditing his memory against theirs. What it shows is narrower and still weighty. Three years after his conversion Paul lodged for a fortnight with Cephas, the first name in the creed; fourteen years later he deliberately “set before” James, Cephas and John the gospel he had been preaching (Galatians 2:2), and they “added nothing” to it and gave him “the right hand of fellowship” (2:6, 9) — requiring nothing further of him and recognizing his gospel as one with their own. The dispute there was about the terms on which Gentiles could be included, not a line-by-line audit of the tradition. So the message Paul preached independently was set before the leading men of the Jerusalem church, those who had known Jesus, and was endorsed by them rather than corrected. The line from the events to the creed does not vanish into anonymous hands; it runs through named people who had access to one another and to the events. So the objection corrects an overstatement, but the link stands in its narrower form.
